claim: Critical thinking is defined in competing ways (Dewey reflective testing of belief; Ennis reasonable reflective thinking for deciding what to believe or do; Facione Delphi purposeful self-regulatory judgment). Ennis alone counted 17 definitions by 2016. No single operational definition exists.
agent_test: Not testable directly; use the Delphi six skills as the label set for scaffold audits.
audit_note: SEP (Hitchcock) says Ennis (2016) lists 17 definitions (14 scholarly plus 3 dictionary); SEP stresses they are conceptions of one concept, so 'no single operational definition' is a mild gloss; Dewey and Facione Delphi wording verified.

claim: The 1990 APA Delphi panel (46 experts, six rounds) agreed on six core skills (interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, self-regulation) and split on dispositions: 61% inclusive vs about 30% procedural-only.
agent_test: Audit result: explanation and an interpretation-fidelity check are the weakest of the six skills in the schema; test a back-translation check at S1.
audit_note: Delphi Report (Facione 1990) confirms 46 experts, six rounds, six core skills, 61% vs 30% split; only one independent document opened (the other listed items are the same report or the local SCHEMA.md).

claim: Ideal critical thinkers are described by dispositions (inquisitiveness, open-mindedness, wanting evidence, willingness to suspend judgment) as well as skills; 19 dispositions in the Delphi list.
agent_test: Ablate disposition-like guardrails (suspend judgment, seek disconfirming evidence) at equal tokens.
audit_note: Delphi Table 5 lists 19 affective dispositions (12 + 7) and SEP discusses skills versus dispositions; 'wanting evidence' is a paraphrase of diligence in seeking relevant information.

claim: Whether CT is general or subject-specific stays contested: McPeck says subject-specific; Delphi says skills transcend subjects but need domain knowledge; transfer evidence is scanty.
agent_test: Test a general critique operator vs domain-primed critique on held-out domains at equal tokens.

claim: CT training programs mostly improve performance on practiced problem types; transfer needs domain knowledge and metacognitive strategies, and many evaluations lack controls.
agent_test: Compare a generic CT prompt vs worked analogous examples on transfer problems.

claim: Human instruction effects: Abrami 2015 meta-analysis of 341 effect sizes found mean g+ = 0.30 (verified from the abstract record); dialogue, authentic problems and mentoring helped most. Huber and Kuncel: skills and dispositions improve substantially over college, curriculum-wide programs add no steady gain; the 0.59 SD and 50th to 72nd percentile figure is still unconfirmed.
agent_test: Not applicable to a frozen model; background only.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction without an external signal does not help and often hurts: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (3 calls) and 41.8 (5 calls); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels it helps (GPT-3.5 CSQA 89.7). Confirmed against the paper. 2025 update: CorrectBench finds intrinsic correction task-dependent (GPT-3.5 Self-Refine HotpotQA -14.21, GSM8K -5.14, GPQA +10.88) and marginal on strong reasoning-trained models; single-utterance correction of injected errors works in open models; parallel voting beats extended rethinking by up to 20%. No certainty-gated re-run of Huang found.
agent_test: Run critique-and-revise with and without an external check (tool, test) at equal tokens; count right-to-wrong flips.

claim: LLM critique is weak: PaLM-2-L got only 54.14% on Critic-HumanEval; critique accuracy tracks answer certainty; filtering votes with self-check adds 0.5 to 1.4 points on GSM8K (ChatGPT 83.5 to 84.0, PaLM-2 91.3 to 92.7). ProcessBench adds false-alarm figures: on correct solutions strong critics are right 91 to 98% of the time (o1-mini 97.9% GSM8K, 95.1% MATH; GPT-4o 91.2% and 76.6%) while weak small models score under 10%.
agent_test: Gate critique to low-certainty items only; compare to always-critique at equal tokens.

claim: Models find reasoning errors poorly but fix them well once located (GPT-4 step-level mistake finding 52.87% direct), so locating errors is the bottleneck.
agent_test: Give the agent a step-error locator; test correction with and without the location.

claim: Models seldom notice faulty or impossible premises unprompted; prompting to check raises recognition sharply (FPBench GPT-4.1 0.23 to 0.81; no-correct-option multiple choice: most models under 15%). Instruction tuning made it worse (Qwen2-Math 0.965 base vs 0.08 instruct).
agent_test: Add an explicit well-posed-question check at intake; measure on no-correct-option items at equal tokens.
audit_note: FPBench GPT-4.1 PRER 0.23 vs PAER 0.81 confirmed; BAD paper numbers (Qwen-Math-7B base 0.965 vs instruct 0.08, most models under 15% in standard/hard) were read through the arXiv v1 HTML summary and the PDF table was garbled; the paper says instruction tuning 'often/tended to' reduce reflective judgment while alignment restored it, so the unqualified 'instruction tuning made it worse' is a slight generalisation.

claim: Assistants cave to pushback. FlipFlop (10 models, 67,640 runs): 46% of answers flipped, 17% mean accuracy drop; every model flips wrong answers more than right ones (GPT-4 30.3% vs 10.4%) yet still flips many right ones. Sharma et al.: 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3) changed answer. In 2026, 8 of 9 reasoning models are more consistent than GPT-4o, but Claude 4.5 is not (average accuracy under attack 86.31% vs 91.29%). Fine-tuning cut the loss about 60%; a third-person prompt raised Turn of Flip on debate items but not on false-presupposition items.
agent_test: Run an are-you-sure probe on initially correct and initially wrong answers; report flip rate on each. Compare plain, third-person prompt, and code-level stance hold at equal tokens.
audit_note: All numbers verified: FlipFlop 67,640 runs, 46% flipped, 17% drop, GPT-4 wrong-flip 30.3% vs correct-flip 10.4%, fine-tuning 9.5% to 3.8% (60% cut); Sharma 32% to 86%; Li et al. 8 of 9 and 86.31% vs 91.29%; SYCON third-person prompt helps debate, no clear trend on false presupposition.

claim: o1-preview scored above humans on structured CT tests (Ennis-Weir 24.33 of 29 vs 11.51 undergraduate, 18.39 postgraduate) but far below on computational problem solving (1.00 vs 3.68). Human comparisons are weak (mismatched cohorts, 3 to 10 trials).
agent_test: Use Ennis-Weir as a scored CT essay probe with a blinded judge; 10+ runs per arm.

claim: Structured critical-question loops give small gains: CQoT lifted MT-Bench reasoning scores by about 0.15 to 0.45 points; generating good critical questions remains hard (no model above 56% useful).
agent_test: Implement an 8-question checkpoint; compare against self-consistency at equal tokens.

claim: Reasoning models over-flag fallacies (more false positives) yet classify them better once a fallacy is known; fallacy detection is subjective and zero-shot LLMs trail humans at fine taxonomy levels.
agent_test: Measure the false-alarm rate of the critique operator on benign text.
audit_note: SmartyPat-Bench (reasoning models over-flag with high FPR yet excel at categorisation) and MAFALDA (subjective annotation; humans outperform LLMs on a 20-example sample) support it; 'at fine taxonomy levels' is not explicit, and the human comparison rests on only 20 examples.

claim: Heavy generative-AI reliance goes with less reported critical thinking: Lee et al. N=319, confidence in AI beta=-0.69; EEG study 54 then 18 participants. Both are correlational or small. Gerlich N=666, r about -0.68 is unverified and has a published correction.
agent_test: Human-side evidence; relevant to interface design, not agent scaffold.

claim: LLM benchmarks treat critical thinking mostly as critique ability, and philosophers found LMs unhelpful partly because they lack a stance and echo the user.
agent_test: Test a stance-holding guardrail against an agreeable baseline on adversarial pushback items.

claim: Schema coverage of the Delphi six skills: three have code-checked gates (evaluation, inference, self-regulation); explanation rests on one model-written line, and interpretation (S1) has no fidelity check. Resisting social pressure has no guardrail.
agent_test: Test S1 back-translation check and a stance-hold rule against plain at equal tokens.

claim: A critique operator's false-alarm rate depends strongly on model strength: on correct math solutions o1-mini wrongly flags 2.1% (GSM8K) and 4.9% (MATH), GPT-4o 8.8% and 23.4%, small open models up to 90+% or none at all.
agent_test: Measure the critic's flag rate on known-correct items before enabling it; report token cost per critique.

claim: Stance cues help only where the stance is an opinion or ethical position; on false-presupposition items prompts (You, Andrew, non-sycophantic) leave Turn of Flip at 1.4 to 3.4 of 5, so premise checking and stance holding are separate fixes.
agent_test: Evaluate the two guardrails separately on false-premise and pushback items.

claim: Prompted intrinsic correction transfers unevenly across tasks (same method: GPQA +10.88, MATH +7.74, HotpotQA -14.21, CS-QA -12.25 for GPT-3.5 Self-Refine); no direct test of a general CT prompt versus domain-primed prompt exists in what we found.
agent_test: Run general vs domain-primed critique on held-out domains at equal tokens.

claim: Stated confidence is not a reliable gate against pressure: confidence-aware generation fails on reasoning models because long traces make them overconfident; random confidence embedding beat targeted extraction.
agent_test: Gate stance on code checks, not on self-reported certainty.
